en: Śrīḥ!

The Compendium of the Essence of the Tantras: All the works of the venerable Lord Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Homage to Śrī Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is identical with Śrī Hanumān, Abhinava Madhva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
First Chapter.
Victorious is the Lord of Kamalā, worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra, who possesses the excellent qualities of infinite majesty, bliss, power, knowledge, and so forth. || 1 ||
Having established the ritual at the beginning of creation, the lotus-eyed Lord,
whose sprout-like feet were shining upon the lap of Rāmā, was questioned by him and spoke.
I alone am the possessor of all qualities, and the Praṇava is my designator;
beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the 'Atiśānta', this is considered my eight-syllabled mantra.
It is the designator of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—the threefold self; of the inner selves; of those united with the knowledge of the Supreme Self; and of my own forms.
The various forms of that [nature] are my other fifty manifestations;
they are denoted by the fifty letters, which are further differentiated by the vowels and the ocean of consonants.
Twice eight, five, four, and five—thus are the letters distributed among the eight groups: Aja, Ānanda, Indra, Īśa, Anuga, Ūrja, Ṛtumbhara, [and Ṛtu]. (6)
He who is the essence of the vowels ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ; the sustainer of vital energy (ojas) and the inner strength (aurasa);
the end, the half-embryo, and the tawny-hued one (kapila); the lord of the sky and he whose seat is Garuḍa. || 7 ||
Gharma, Ṅasāra, Cārvaṅga, Chandogamya, Janārdana;
Jhāṭitāri, Ñamaṣṭaṅkī, Ṭhalaka, Ḍalaka, and Ḍharī.

He is the Self, the one situated in the sun, the bearer of the staff, the wielder of the bow, the one to be saluted, the Supreme, the possessor of fruit, the powerful one, the fortunate one, Manu, the sacrifice, Rāma, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Excellent One. || 9 ||
The peaceful consciousness, the one endowed with the six qualities, the essential self, the *haṃsa*, and the *lāluka*—these are my fifty forms, characterized by the letters beginning with 'A'. (10)
The eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa is distinguished by the eight-syllable mantra of Tārā;
in the former, it is differentiated by the first four syllables of Tārā, while the Vyāhṛtis follow in sequence.
Their deities are Aniruddha and the others, either in regular or reverse order;
these indeed possess four forms, as expressed by the twelve-syllable words.
From the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa and likewise from the vyāhṛtis, the twelve-syllabled mantras are differentiated; Keśava and the others are their presiding deities. (13)
Furthermore, from the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa and the three-fold Vyāhṛtis,
the Mother of the Vedas, Gāyatrī, arises as twelve-syllabled and double that [in power].
Her twenty-four forms are declared to be the deities of the phonemes;
their Veda is said to be the Puruṣa-sūkta, and the Vedas are contained within that Puruṣa-hymn.
And since all Vedic words [originate] from that, I am the designator of everything;
furthermore, all words are distinguished by the fifty phonemes.
I am the seer and the deity for Tārā and the others specifically; my metre is considered to be Gāyatrī for both Tārā and the eight-syllable mantra. (17)
Resplendent with the luster of the rising sun, possessing a singular body of consciousness and bliss, bearing the discus, conch, mace, and lotus—I am the Lord to be meditated upon. 18.
Embraced by Lakṣmī and Dhara, he stands in the midst of his own host of forms,
together with Brahmā, Vāyu, Śiva, the Lord of Serpents, Viṣṇu, and also Indra and the other gods.

Being served with excessive devotion, He who possesses eternal and infinite power—His eight forms should also be meditated upon, endowed with the discus, conch, boon-granting gesture, and gesture of fearlessness;
they are the color of lamps and adorned with all ornaments. (20)

And fifty [deities] of such form, raising their hands in the *jñānamudrā* and the gesture of fearlessness, are joined with their respective [consorts] on the left—[the male deities] being the wielder of the axe (*ṭaṅkin*), the wielder of the staff (*daṇḍin*), and the wielder of the bow (*dhanvin*). (21)
Vāsudeva and the others are brilliant with white, red, yellow, and black complexions;
the first holds a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, while the others hold a mace and a plow.
The second is accompanied by the conch and discus; the third possesses the Śārṅga bow and arrows;
the fourth, however, possesses the conch and discus, as well as the discus, conch, sword, and shield.
Keśava, Madhusūdana,
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, and Pradyumna hold a staff, a raised hand, and a conch shell.
Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Aniruddha, Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, and Janārdana are considered to be those who hold a conch and a discus in their left and right hands respectively. (25)
Govinda, Trivikrama, Śrīdhara,
Hṛṣīkeśa, Nṛsiṃha, and Acyuta are those whose left lower hand holds a conch.
Vāmana, Sanārāyaṇa, Padmanābha, Upendraka, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa are considered to hold the conch in their lower right hands. (27)
Indeed, these [deities] all hold the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;

likewise, there is the sequential order, the reverse order, the sequence beginning with the lotus and the mace, the reverse sequence, the half-sequence, and the sequence with intervals—these six [arrangements] for those whose enemies begin with the six [groups]. 28.
Because the phonemes and the deities are eternal, there is no sequence inherent in them;
rather, a sequence is spoken of only with reference to the order of their manifestation as perceived by the intellect of Brahmā. (29)
Through the method of both concise and detailed exposition, the four Vyāhṛtis,
Satya, the limbs of Tāra, and those of the eight-syllabled mantra are proclaimed.
Those ending in the dative case—namely *kṛtvam*, *mahāvīra*, *dyutka*, *sahasrahita*, and *ulkaka*—are the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others; they are also distinct forms. (31)
Although there is no difference between these [forms] and Viṣṇu himself, due to his sovereign power they appear like others;
in all of them, the hands hold the discus, the conch, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
The crest is said to be black in color, matching the color of the original form;
likewise, the twenty-four forms are of the same color as the original form.
The first three syllables should be deposited, in due order, upon the navel, the heart, and the head, preceded by meditation on their respective deities. (34)
The placement of the eight-syllabled Vyāhṛtis should be performed by Prajāpati upon the knees, navel, heart, speech, nose, and eyes. (35)
The sage is Gāyatrī, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Blessed Lord Hari;
he has the color of the rising sun and displays the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) with his hands raised in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). || 36 ||
The five limbs are to be known [by worship] with the syllable *Tāra* (Om) and the *Vyāhṛtis*.
One should place the four *Vyāhṛtis* in all the locations: the navel, the heart, and the head.
For the twelve-syllable mantra, the meter is remembered as Jagatī, like that of the Tāra-mantra;
he of immeasurable luster should be meditated upon as having a white complexion and hands granting fearlessness and boons. (38)
The five limbs are to be known by means of the words both individually and collectively;
one should place them in the locations of the eight syllables, namely the two arms and the two thighs. (39)
But Viśvāmitra, the Lord of Creatures, is for the sake of the twilight;
the sage is the god named Savitṛ, and because of his creative power, he is Hari. (40)
Having the color of the rising sun, situated in the midst of the solar orb, bearing the discus and the conch, with two arms resting upon his lap—he is indeed to be meditated upon. (41)

The *vyāhṛtis* together with the stars (the seven *ṛṣis*) and the five limbs of the *gāyatrī* [should be placed] on the joints of the arms and feet, including their tips, as well as on the navel, the heart, and the face. 42.
The placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) should be performed as before; it is taught that this applies entirely to all fifty letters and also to the Puruṣasūkta in its entirety. (43)
The Anuṣṭubh and Triṣṭubh are its meters, or it may be in the Triṣṭubh meter;
the word "Viṣṇu" ending in the dative case follows the word "hṛdaya," forming a six-syllable mantra.
Just as in the case of Tāra, for this [mantra] as well, Hari himself is to be meditated upon as Śyāma;
the six syllables themselves constitute the six limbs through the application of the distinction between the two [mantras].
The placement [of mantras] syllable by syllable upon the feet, knees, navel, heart, nose, and hair-tuft—these, in particular, are the root-mantras of all mantras. (46)
Through the knowledge of this, everything within the scope of speech becomes known;
through the recitation of this, one becomes a reciter of all mantras. (47)
And the Blessed One should be worshipped constantly within a maṇḍala such as the wheel or the lotus, or in the heart, or in a moving object, or in water, or on bare ground. 48.
Having first worshipped the supreme deity with the eight-syllable mantra,
one should worship the gurus in the center, and all the deities on the right.
Again, on the left and in the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneyī) and so forth,
one should place in order Garuḍa, Vyāsadeva, Durgā, and Sarasvatī.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya located in the corners; within that, one should first worship Adharma and the others in the directions starting from the east.
Those who bestow unrighteousness and the like when they have not been worshipped are designated by those names;
Nirṛti, Durgā, Kāma, and Rudra are their presiding deities.
Yama, Vāyu, Śiva, and Indra are to be known as the deities of Dharma and the other [directions];
the Supreme Puruṣa is in the center, and Śakti has the form of the foundation.
The Tortoise, Ananta, the Earth, the Ocean of Milk, Śvetadvīpa, and the great jeweled pavilion made of divine gems.
O Goddess, this triad of lotuses is Rāmā herself in her manifold forms;
within the lotuses are the Sun, the Moon, and the Fire, while Śrī is the embodiment of the three guṇas.
The forms are the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self;
likewise, they are Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā. (56)
Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and Anugrahā are the Śaktis;
they are the very forms of Hari himself in the eight directions and in the center.
Then one should worship the infinite nature of the Yoga-pīṭha of Hari;
having invoked Hari there, [one should offer] the arghya, pādya, and ācamanīya.
Furthermore, having offered the madhuparka, water for sipping (ācamana), a bath, clothing, ornaments, the sacred thread (upavīta), a seat, as well as fragrant paste and flowers; || 59 ||
There, in the Lakṣmīgṛha, one should worship the two sides of Hari;
likewise, the Hṛdaya-mantra and others in the directions starting with Indra, and the Astra-mantra in the corners.
Then, one should place Vāsudeva and the others in the cardinal directions, followed by Keśava and the rest;
then Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana.
One should worship Bhārgava, Rāghava, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki, as well as Ananta and Viśvarūpa, outside of that in due order.
One should first worship Ananta, Brahmā, Vāyu, Īśa, and Īśa [Śiva],
as well as Vāruṇī, Gāyatrī, Bhāratī, and Girijā.
One should also worship Suparṇī in the corners and to the left of Viṣṇu,
as well as Indra and the others, ending with Śeṣa, together with their wives and retinues.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) with the root mantra;
by this sequential method, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the consecrated fire.
The offering of a handful of flowers and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
for other [mantras], the flower offering is done once each, while the homa is four times that amount.

Having offered the food oblation (naivedya) and worshipped three times with the root mantra, and having again presented incense and lamps, one should worship once more with the root mantra as before. || 67 ||
Having worshipped and meditated again, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
first, one should meditate upon Hari, the Lord of all gods and the sovereign Master.
He who always performs recitation, meditation, burnt offerings, and so forth in this manner, shall indeed become a vessel for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (69)
Having known Hari as the most supreme, whoever constantly worships him with devotion through recitation, meditation, and other means—for such a person, nothing is difficult to attain. (70)
Having offered devotion even to other deities such as Brahmā and Rudra,
without recognizing the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu, one certainly goes to darkness.
Neither sacrifices, nor sacred fords, nor fasts and vows, nor all the deities together, would ever be able to protect him. (72)
For Hari is the supreme among all gods, possessed of perfect power;
he is independent, while all others are under his control. Therefore, he is the teacher of the world.
And through devotion to Him, even Brahmā and the others partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, Hari is always to be known, worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon. (74)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tantrasārasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The Second Chapter:
The placement (nyāsa) of any mantra whatsoever with five syllables bestows vigor; [these are placed] on the forehead, all around, the mouth, the eyes, the ears, and the two nostrils.
On the two cheeks, the two lips, the rows of teeth, the head, and the speech; on the joints of the arms and feet, including their tips, on the two sides, the back, and the private parts. || 2 ||

One should place the letters beginning with *kṣa* in the navel, the heart, the seven elements, and in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*); Nṛsiṃha is the deity of the letter *kṣa*.
In the performance of *japa* and *nyāsa*, the syllable *kṣaḥ* is always prescribed at the end;
likewise, one should perform *prāṇāyāma* after exhaling and filling [the breath] during the retention (*kumbhaka*).
It should be performed with three, twelve, or two, one, and twelve repetitions of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*),
or with the respective mantra, or with the *gāyatrī* and ten *tāras*.
At the very beginning of the recitation (japa), one should perform the drying, burning, and flooding [of the mantra];
having meditated upon Hari within that mandala by means of the seed-syllables of Vāyu, Agni, and Varuṇa.
There are twenty-four forms for the fifty-one syllables:
those beginning with Ātman, those beginning with Vāsudeva, those beginning with Viśva, and [the forms] Matsya and Kacchapa.
Kola was Nṛsiṃha; Savaṭi was the son of Jamadagni and the upholder of the Raghu lineage;
Vasiṣṭha and Yadu were the two Kṛṣṇas; and Ātreya was both Buddha and Kalkin.
And the Śiṃśumāra—these one hundred digits (kalās) are named after the pitcher (kalaśa).
A wise man, together with these, [should place them] in the water of the pitcher before the primary image (mūlamūrti).

Having worshipped the image and the disciple according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should first bathe them; for the worship, the recitation of mantras should not be less than a thousand times.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the root mantra and its limbs, performed immediately after bathing,
brings about the presence [of the deity] in the image and effects greatness in the disciple.
The water-pot (kalaśa) shall accomplish renown, longevity, wisdom, intelligence, prosperity, strength, fitness, the destruction of sins, and the increase of merit. || 12 ||
When calamities have arisen—whether caused by fate, spirits, or one's own self—for the sake of longevity, or for peace, or for prosperity, or for the increase of merit; || 13 ||
For the sake of fitness, for the perfection of the mantra, or indeed for the pleasure of Viṣṇu,
one should offer oblations a thousand times, ten thousand times, a hundred thousand times, or even ten million times.
As before, having meditated upon the god Janārdana in the consecrated fire,
one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with three ridges and twenty-four finger-breadths in height.
It should be square, elevated, and twelve units in size, measuring either two, three, or four finger-breadths [in height]. || 16 ||
The width of the girdles should be four finger-breadths at the end;
their width may also be twenty-four finger-breadths or twelve. || 17 ||
It should have the shape of an aśvattha leaf; from the base, it is twelve finger-breadths long, and the yoni is curved inward, entering two finger-breadths into the excavation.
Then, having meditated upon Hari within himself and likewise upon the goddess Śrī in the sacrificial pit,
he should indeed cast into it the fire whose essence is the seed of Viṣṇu while reciting the Praṇava.
One should perform the sixteen rites individually with the Vyāhṛtis;
then, bringing satisfaction to Agni and that Lord of the Cave (the Sun), one should worship Him with offerings.
Or with clarified butter, or with milk-rice, or with fuel-sticks of trees that yield milky sap;
or else with wood-apples, or even with rice grains, or indeed with the three sweet substances alone.
Or with fuel-sticks of the Brahma-tree, or with fuel-sticks produced from the Amṛta plant;
these should be known as Amṛta-fuel-sticks, four finger-breadths long in every case.
In this very manner, during initiation, the performance of oblations with clarified butter and the worship must be conducted according to the rules, even prior to all other burnt offerings.
The wise man should give a hundred-fold fee to the preceptor for every hundred thousand recitations;
likewise, when the homa is performed by himself, he should give a guru-dakṣiṇā according to his capacity.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Tantrasārasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter: A wise man, while performing the consecration of Viṣṇu, should have a beautiful image made,
using metal, stone, wood, or even clay, according to the prescribed order.
In the Yoga practice, for those seeking liberation, one should describe one's own state as being ninety-six finger-breadths [in height], whether sitting, standing, or lying down. (2)
Above the mouth, it is two finger-breadths high; its face shines with nine finger-breadths;
its well-rounded neck is three finger-breadths; and from the neck to the breasts, it measures six finger-breadths.
It is fifteen finger-breadths from the navel to the mouth,
and it extends for two and a half finger-breadths from the scrotum to its base.
First, from the anus, it should extend eighteen finger-breadths upward from the *caitya*;
then, with a *caitya* of two finger-breadths, it should be joined with the shank for twenty-two [finger-breadths].
Starting from the middle of the ankle, [the length] is three and a half finger-breadths;
the forefoot is six finger-breadths in height, and its thickness is exactly two and a half finger-breadths.
At the end, it should be joined with the raised forepart of the foot (prapada), with a height of two finger-breadths for the prapada;
the middle finger-breadth should be three, two, or even half a finger-breadth less.
Then, the other [toes] are three finger-breadths shorter; likewise, the next [toe] is similar;
the big toe's nail is one-quarter of a finger-breadth high, and the space between them is half of that.
Gradually decreasing by one-quarter [of a digit], it is auspicious with red-colored toenails;
the width of the forepart of the foot (prapada) is said to be six digits.
The circumference of the thumb is said to be four finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
that of the other [fingers] is three finger-breadths; and the subsequent [joints] are successively less by half a grain of rice.
The base of the calf is ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas), while the middle part is three finger-breadths more;
the upper part is seventeen finger-breadths, and the knee is eighteen finger-breadths.

The thighs should be known to be likewise; the middle part is twenty-four finger-breadths (dvādaśa-aṅgula) [twice twelve], the root is four finger-breadths more, and the secret part is four and a half.
The scrotum is said to be three and a half [aṅgulas] in circumference and four aṅgulas in length;
it is described as being entirely circular with a circumference of seven aṅgulas.
The circumference of the waist is declared to be thirty-eight finger-breadths;
likewise, the hips should be perfectly rounded and plump in every respect. (14)
Likewise, the width of the hips and the well-established nature of the feet [are to be considered];
it is taught that the measurement below the navel exceeds that of the hips by one finger-breadth.
The navel is one and a half finger-breadths deep and half a finger-breadth high;
it is circular, spiraling to the right, and measures forty-two finger-breadths [in circumference].
The circumference of the breast at its center is six finger-breadths, or more;
the characteristic measurement for the width of that chest is nineteen finger-breadths. || 17 ||
The width of each shoulder, including the two arms, is considered to be three and a half finger-breadths,
while the span across the shoulders is separately regarded as eight finger-breadths.
The height from the armpit to the shoulders is considered to be seven finger-breadths;
the measurement of the two hands is said to be thirty-eight finger-breadths.
The circumference of the two upper arms is stated to be eighteen finger-breadths;
at their ends, however, it is said to be gradually reduced to eight and a half finger-breadths.
The palm [of the hand] with its fingers is declared to be nine fingers including the thumb;
both of these should be known as equal, and the same applies to the width of the palm. || 21 ||
The middle finger is raised half a finger-breadth; those two [the ring and little fingers] are raised by one and a half finger-breadths;
and for that little finger, the next [measurement] is increased by the size of a grain of rice.
The middle and the largest [measures] are declared to have a circumference of three and a half [units];
the other two are one and a half and half of that [respectively], while another is two and a half finger-breadths.
All [the measurements] except for the height of the head are recorded as being three-quarters of the circumference;
likewise, the circumference of the neck is equal to the width of the chest. (24)
The forehead, the belly, and the neck should be endowed with three long lines;
likewise, the neck, the arms, the breasts, and the fingers should be rounded.
The palms, nails, the corners of the eyes, the lower lip, the upper lip, and the tongue are red; and the nails are slightly shorter than the fingers. (26)
The two middle [fingers] are likewise half a finger [in width], while the others decrease by one-eighth part in sequence;
below the nose is the nose itself, and then the forehead.
The nose shall be measured by the same unit as the face in terms of its height;
indeed, the entire [length] of the face will be one-half finger-breadth more. (28)

Likewise, its mouth is known to be four finger-breadths wide; the lower lip is said to be one and a half grains of rice in thickness, while the upper lip is the measure of a single grain of rice, and that which is above it is like the lower lip.
The lower lip is said to be one and a half finger-breadths below [the upper lip],
and the two sides of the mouth are said to extend six finger-breadths from the ear.
The side of the nose from the tip to the ear is said to be seven finger-breadths; the height of the nose is proclaimed to be one and a quarter finger-breadths.
The nostril-cavity is said to be half a finger-breadth in width, and its middle part likewise; the nose is as wide as a grain of rice, and the two eyes are three fingers apart.
The two ears should be one finger-breadth wide and full-blown; otherwise, they should be half that size.
The two eyebrows should be four finger-breadths long and half a finger-breadth wide.
The eyelashes are unseparated, dense, and beautifully dark blue;
the ears measure three finger-breadths in length and are endowed with a width of two and a half finger-breadths. (34)
The opening, together with the two earrings, is proclaimed to be exactly that much; likewise, its width is said to be two finger-breadths along with the two creepers.
Her ears were adorned with ear-ornaments and joined by two blue lotuses;
her lotus-face was graced by a thousand dark tresses of hair. (36)
The forehead is very broad, measuring nine and a half finger-breadths;
the head is circular at its base and is known to be shaped like an umbrella.
The hair of Hari is considered to be long, with curled tips and dark blue;
indeed, the crown of Keśava is as high as the measurement of his face.
The two earrings are shaped like sea-monsters (makara), and the chest, adorned with the Kaustubha gem and the Śrīvatsa mark,
is described as being full and elevated on the right side.
It was likewise provided with necklaces, neck-ornaments, and sacred threads,
as well as arms adorned with bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings.
A yellow garment was tied at the waist with a girdle, while her hips were adorned with it; and upon her feet were anklets of exceedingly sweet sound.
One should have well-fashioned toe-rings for the feet made by skilled artisans;
and [the image] should be provided with an upper garment and equipped with weapons such as the discus and others.
It should be endowed with a beautiful smile characterized by teeth that are neither protruding nor uneven; it should possess an even gaze, be smooth, and truly captivating.
Accompanied by five auspicious sounds, he should proceed for the sake of the image;
having gone to a pure spot, he should there examine the stone.
Having discerned by the difference in sound that the stone contains an embryo, one should abandon it;
reciting the root mantra and meditating on Viṣṇu, one should remain fasting.
If it is made of wood, one should have it fashioned from the heartwood of a sacrificial tree;
and the offering of the bali-oblation is now described according to the concise procedure.
Because this is a compendium of teachings, it does not contradict detailed expositions.
Having offered an oblation to Hari, one should present the sacrificial portion (bali) to those beings who are his manifestations.
Having taken [the offerings] from the eastern Viṣṇubhūtas, and so forth in all directions, as well as from the Viṣṇubhūtas, the Lokapālas, and likewise from Hari; 48.
Having obtained permission, one should uproot a tree or a stone for the purpose of making an image;
the image, its pedestal, and its base may be fashioned from stones of the three types.
According to the distinction of tone and thickness, stones are classified by genders such as male and female;
one should take a male stone for the sake of the image and a female stone for the construction of the pedestal.
Accompanied by the auspicious sounds of the Vedas and musical instruments, one should carry the image [there];
the wise man should then construct a temple in a location sloping toward the east or the north.
To the south of the Rāmā river, behind it, or even on the very peak of the mountain; or in the center of a large and very pure village or city. || 52 ||
In the northeastern direction alone, in a place devoid of water, or in the middle of a body of water that is free from stones, trees, and the like; || 53 ||
One should construct a place for the residence of the deity at a distance from places such as cremation grounds, in a region that is pleasant and beautiful, measuring no less than twelve *kiṣkus*.
Having properly performed the purification of the ground to a depth of two, four, or even a hundred cubits, one should place [the vessel] below at a depth of one and a half man-lengths.
In a place free from hair, charcoal, bones, anthills, clods of earth, stones, and the like,
one should worship Hari there as well and offer the oblation (bali) as before.
One should construct a firm temple out of clay, wood, stone, or metals. The [measurement] rods should be three *kalamas* in length, with eight barley grains' width across.
They are traditionally said to be equal in measure to the middle line of one's own finger;
indeed, the middle line of one's own finger is the standard for images and the like. (58)
The respective measurements for each [type] in their entirety are distinguished as small, medium, and large;
the general characteristic is that they are measured by a span (prādeśa), a cubit (hasta), or a man’s height (puruṣa).
The width of the door should be half the height of the image, and its height should be equal to the middle part [of the image];
the height of the pedestal is desired to be half the measurement of the image.
The elevation of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should measure four aṅgulas;
it may also be three or two aṅgulas, equal to the interior of the temple or the height of the image.

The height and the width [of the base] are specified in sequence; it is remembered that the middle portion is of medium height, and if it is a single-peaked structure, it should be as high externally as that [middle portion].
Alternatively, it may be half as high [as the base], or elevated at the bottom;
or its measure may be double that, or even one and a half times the height of the image.
The measurement of the image on the interior of the pinnacle is said to be its neck;
it should be three-quarters, half, or even one and a half times that [measurement]. (64)
The vimāna is proclaimed to be circular like a lotus, or likewise like the back of an elephant, as well as quadrangular or octagonal. 65.
The pinnacle should be ten or even twenty times the size of the image;
it should be circular and shaped like a crown.
Whether it be provided with a courtyard, or even separate courtyards, or two courtyards, or three courtyards, or even with a gateway (gopura). || 67 ||
It may be endowed with various types of arrangements, or consist of exactly seven types;
it is a Sahma-vṛtta (square) measuring one cubit, or it may be square on the outside.
Beyond that, if the interior of the assembly hall is only one cubit (kiṣku),
then it is declared that the third [hall] should be exactly half of that measure.
The Kiṣkutraka is the abode of Śakra and others, as is traditionally taught according to its application;
from that, one should construct the Maṇṭapa, which possesses the auspicious characteristics for the consecration.
The son of Hari, Vāstuvarāha, always worships the gods beginning with Brahmā who reside above the Vāstupuruṣa.
Cast down to the earth by the deities, he remained there in a square shape; having divided it into eight times eight squares, Brahmā was placed in the center of the four [central squares].
Śakra, Yama, and Varuṇa are to be worshipped in each pair [of directions], as is Soma;
and the deities of the corners, beginning with Agni, are to be worshipped in the corners.
Furthermore, one should worship the three [gods] in the triad—the Sustainer (Dhātṛ) along with the Ordainer (Vidhātṛ), Skanda, and likewise Sūrya and Vināyaka—in the corner. (74)
One should worship Kāla and Kubera outside, each in their respective directions; and Hārin, Hari, Gabhīra, Gāhana, Gahana, and Guha. (75)
One should worship Bhānu and Maṅgāraka in the eastern direction;
as well as Dāruma, Vidari, Dyota, Pradyota, Dyotana, and Hira. (76)
One should worship Mṛtyu and Śanaiścara in the southern direction;
[and] Puṣkara, Kṣaraṇa, Kṣārin, Vikṣaṇa, Kṣobhaṇa, and Kṣaṇa. || 77 ||
One should worship Cārvaṅga and Bhārgava in the western direction;
[and likewise] Cāra, Vicāra, Pracāra, Sañcāra, Caraṇa, and Cara.
One should worship Bṛhaspati and Budha in the north;
likewise, one should worship them even before the construction of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Then, one should skillfully construct a pavilion made of *saptaparṇa* wood,
measuring seven cubits, twelve cubits, or twice that [twenty-four] cubits.
One should properly construct a square courtyard four times [the size of the original],
and furthermore, one should have another long pavilion made measuring five cubits.
Therein, one should properly construct an auspicious maṇḍala consisting of three by four squares, extending eastward in the center, measuring exactly one cubit in width.
There, one should place twelve vessels, such as *pālikās* and others;
the *pālikās*, moreover, should be endowed with a height of twenty-four finger-breadths.
They are eighteen finger-breadths long and likewise have five faces;
the shallow bowls (śarāva) following behind are twelve finger-breadths long.
There, one should worship Viṣṇu in his fourfold form with devotion three times;
one should fill those very [vessels] with seven kinds of grain for the purpose of the sprouting ceremony.
There, one should constantly offer an oblation for ten nights to Viṣaṇu,
as well as to Brahmā, Śaṅkara, the gods, the ancestors, the Gandharvas, and the Yakṣas.

And with the Bhūtas, one should worship in due order with milk-rice (pāyasa), lotus-seeds and unbroken rice (akṣata), food and cakes, food and flowers, food and parched grain with unbroken rice, and groats; or alternatively, up to the Devas, with milk-rice alone.
At that very time, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of the image;
having immersed it in the five products of the cow for seven nights while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.

The best of the twice-born should properly master the four Vedas; two should be stationed at each of the gates, beginning with the eastern one, while at least ten should be assigned to each. Alternatively, those devoted to Viṣṇu may be appointed according to their availability or their wealth.
The wise man should have thirteen sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed here around [the central area],
endowed with the previously described characteristics; however, the principal one should be in the southeast corner,
at a distance of exactly one cubit from the corner, according to the intelligent one.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) into each of those [fires] by the count of one hundred thousand (lakṣa),
or alternatively, ten thousand (ayuta) for each, while the primary [oblation] consists of one hundred thousand.
Alternatively, the knower of mantras should first offer half of that, or even half of that again, with the root mantra,
for the sake of the twenty-five principles, beginning with Pradhāna.
Either one thousand or one hundred for each [deity],

having first performed the preliminary consecration in water with the Puruṣasūkta and a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, or [the consecration] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 93 ||
In the pavilion, one should prepare an auspicious mandala, either a wheel-lotus (cakrābja) or a "fortunate" (bhadraka) design;
likewise, there should be a lotus, three circles, a wheel, the zodiac signs, and walkways.
The characteristics of the wheel-lotus (cakrābja) include both primary and secondary ornaments;
however, the specific distinction for the Bhadraka type is said to be a wheel that is square.
There, one should worship a thousand, half of that, or a quarter of water-jars;
if there is a lack of wealth, it is said that one may worship a hundred, half of that, or a quarter.
With the decoction of milk-trees, as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
with pure pañcagavya, and with water— each separately.
One should fill the central jar with pure water alone; for the Brahma-jar, there should be four jars of scented water in the four directions. (98)
In the mandala situated as a group of four white four-petalled lotuses,
one should place, according to the sequence starting from the east, juices, decoctions, and auspicious waters.
One should place perfumes and set the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) within a pure vessel;
the wise one, having made small red four-petaled lotuses separately for each. (100)
In the case of five hundred [vessels], however, one should place a vessel of scented water in the very center;
and to the east of the Brahma-vessel, one should establish a large vessel belonging to Śarva.
One should place five [vessels] upon each of the eight lotuses in the eight directions;
by this sequential method, all the jars [are arranged].
One should place vessels made of various substances there on the outside; at that very time, one should arrange the vessels for the sprouts all around that area.
Kuśa-water, camphor, saffron, sandalwood, as well as water with snow, water with turmeric, uśīra-grass, and mustard from a granary; || 104 ||

That which arises at the confluence of rivers, as well as that from a pond, a well, or a mountain spring—these are declared to be the specific types of water-jars (kalaśas). These two kinds of pure water also originate from great sacred fords (tīrthas). 105.
One should invoke the other forms of the twenty-four manifestations within the principle (tattva), according to their colors and forms, both in direct and reverse order.
Furthermore, for the forms of the colors, one should likewise recite the mantras two or four times;
and when there are a thousand jars and so forth, one should recite the mantras according to one's capacity.
Then, having respectfully brought the image with the fivefold sounds and the chanting of the Vedas, one should perform its ritual bathing with the *praṇava*.
With the mantras ending with the Puruṣasūkta, as well as with the Viśvataścakṣus [hymn], and again with the eight-syllabled mantra and the Praṇava, [one should worship] with devotion. || 109 ||
Having bathed [the image] with scented waters and having adorned it again with fragrant flowers and other offerings, one should then install the image with the syllable Om (praṇava).

The practitioner of mantras should likewise recite the eight-syllable mantra and the specific mantra for each respective form one hundred and eight times, while again meditating upon her as consisting of pure light.
Within the image, situated inside the image, is that supreme form in its midst—
the highest essence of consciousness and bliss, completely filled with a fullness of all qualities.
Immediately thereafter, one should install the deities of the twenty-five principles all around Keśava, within the midst of the image.
There, he recited the hymn beginning with "ā tvāhārṣam," the Vaiṣṇava hymn concerning the Gharma, the hymn of Viśvakarman, and indeed the Puruṣa-sūkta. (114)
Having recited his own mantra and again the eight-syllabled one, the wise man should then mutter the *praṇava* while meditating on Viṣṇu of supreme form.
Then, one should bathe Janārdana with jars according to the external sequence using the prescribed mantras, but the central one with the *praṇava*.

The invocation and the bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are likewise performed with his own eight-syllable mantra and from the Puruṣasūkta. The sequence of the pitchers is said to begin from the east and end in the north.
Having again recited those mantras, one should perform worship according to the prescribed rules,
and having offered the ritual oblation (bali) to the guardians of the gates and the world-protectors in due order.

Having adorned the preceptor with garments, jewels, gold, and other riches according to one's wealth, one should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of ten million, a hundred thousand, or a thousand [gold pieces].
One who is destitute should, out of devotion, seek forgiveness by offering one hundred, fifty, or even half of that;
half of that again for the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and half of that for those who perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
One should give food in its entirety to those who have horses and to those who cook for horses,
continuously for seven nights, both before and after [the ritual].
One should also worship those who have arrived as guests with gold, garments, jewels, and other offerings, according to one's ability and with devotion, saying: "May the Blessed One be pleased. (122)
For seven days, [he was honored] with songs, dances, instrumental music, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, as well as with hymns, auspicious proclamations, and Vedic chants.
From this point, the wise one should cause the ceremonial bath (avabhṛtha) of the God of gods to be performed with royal splendor, accompanied by Vedic recitations, songs, and dances. 124.
At the confluence of great rivers, at that most highly praised sacred ford,
one should bathe [the image] as before with mantras ending with the *Puruṣasūkta*, while remembering Hari.
Then, having returned as before and caused Puruṣottama to enter,
he worshipped him according to the prescribed rite and gave gifts according to his capacity.
Having honored the guru with devotion, he should then accept him as his disciple;
furthermore, the food offering (naivedya) should consist of no less than one hundred prasthas.
During these days, one should offer [food] together with ghee, sugar, and other ingredients;
thereafter, worship of Hari should always be performed according to one's capacity. 128.
And upon the removal from a dilapidated abode, having likewise recited the mantras of the principles (tattvas) and his own [mantra] in reverse order, he should dissolve Hari into the image.
According to the very procedure already described, the wise man, having bathed Hari with half that wealth— or even with a quarter of it— as desired, [should proceed].
Having constructed the temple again according to this very same procedure,
one should bathe the Lotus-eyed Lord with double the amount of water used for the procession.
Furthermore, one should likewise please the mantras with an expansive and favorable disposition;
and meditating as prescribed, one should worship the Lord of the World with devotion. (132)
The procession there, as well as in all other festivals, is likewise as before;
the worship and the offering of oblations are performed according to the procedure prescribed for the water-pot (kalaśa).
Festivals should always be performed, and after the festival, the water-pot (kalaśa) [should be honored];
furthermore, the procession and the ritual bath must be carried out according to the correctly prescribed injunctions.
Upon the entry of thieves, Caṇḍālas, outcasts, or menstruating women, and likewise upon defilement by a corpse or the like, as well as upon the interruption of worship; || 135 ||
The performance of expiation is prescribed according to the procedure stated for the ritual bathing;
in all cases, the fire-oblation (homa) with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra should consist of at least ten thousand offerings.
We know the names beginning with *nau* and *avya*, and likewise we meditate upon them; may that which is named *gāyatrī* impel us from beneath the third [syllable]. (137)
One should also install Durgā, Śiva, Skanda, Sūrya, Vināyaka, and others by means of their respective mantras according to the prescribed method, while remembering Hari.
A pair or even a triad of Viṣṇu’s globes (golaka) is prescribed for the consecrations of other deities; in those cases, one should meditate upon Hari within them.
But worship devoid of the recollection of Viṣṇu is likewise demonic;
the deities do not accept it, and from that arises the ruin of the country through disease, thieves, and other calamities. Therefore, Hari should always be meditated upon within.
The destiny of one devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu shall never be auspicious; likewise for one devoted to other deities. Therefore, Hari should always be meditated upon. (141)
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious and the bestower of all desired boons, should be meditated upon by all people; when remembered, he becomes so. (142)

The Person (Puruṣa), the Unmanifest (Avyakta), the Great One (Mahat), the Ego (Ahaṅkāra), the mind (Manas), the ten sense organs, and the five objects of sense such as sound—these constitute the twenty-five principles. || 143 ||
The principles known as Tattva, Kāla, Māyā, Niyati, Mati, Vidya, Kalā, and Pravṛtti constitute the collection of thirty-two principles. 144.
The wise know that there are eleven other forms of Mahālakṣmī, namely Sphūrti, Saṃvit, Pratiṣṭhā, Śakti, and so forth;
for Viṣṇu also has exactly eleven forms bearing those same names. (145)
All of them, even those with two arms, possessed complexions resembling that of the Primal One;
they stood with palms joined in reverence toward that Lord Hari.
All these principles are indeed Brahmā, who is remembered as Puruṣa;
and Mahat, along with the Unmanifest (Avyakta), is proclaimed as Brahmāṇī. || 147 ||
In this way, Vāyu should also be known, as well as Bhāratī; these three constitute that triad.
Rudra is designated as the ego (ahaṅkāra), while Skanda and Indra are said to be the mind (manas). 148.
Ahaṃkāra, Śeṣa, and Vāsava are also declared by the learned;
as well as the quarters, the son of Vāyu, Sūrya, Varuṇa, and both Aśvinī. 149.
Vahni, Dakṣa, Indrasūnu, Mitra, Manu, and the one named Indriya—these are the [sages], and Bṛhaspati is declared to be the name of Śabda. (150)
Furthermore, other sons of Vāyu and Rudra are also proclaimed;
among these, the Blessed Viṣṇu alone is the primary embodiment. 151.
The name of the reality (tattva) should be meditated upon between the supreme self (parātman) and the individual self (ātman), as well as between their respective meanings;
however, in recitation (japa) and ritual placement (nyāsa), it should end with "namaḥ," while in the rite of fire-oblation (homakarma), it should end with "svāhā."
In the rites of oblation and so forth, the repetition of these [mantras] is prescribed as three, four, six, and ten times respectively.
Their placement (nyāsa) on the fingers, thighs, and arms is taught in reverse order;
here, by reversing the sequence, their status as Śakti and the others is proclaimed.

When the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (devatā), and limb-meditation (aṅgadhyāna) are not explicitly stated, they should be understood as being like those of the principal mantra; all such mantras bestow liberation and other benefits individually. || 154 ||
Although countless paths of Tantra have indeed been proclaimed by Hari, among them this path is easy to follow and fruitful for those who practice it. (155)
For as long as there is no performance [of these rites], the fulfillment of karma does not exist; therefore, everything has been explained in this tantra according to the prescribed rule. (156)
By this path, he is pleased; when worshipped, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, becomes the bestower of liberation and the granter of desires to his own devotees. || 157 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Tantrasārasaṅgraha* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The Fourth Chapter. Now, that collection of mantras which was proclaimed by Viṣṇu in the *Tantrasāra* is here stated in brief, together with its complete means of accomplishment.
The eighth [syllable] joined with *tū*, followed by *anta* (the letter *m*), and then the mountain (*bhūbhṛtaḥ*)—that is, *na*;
then the seed-syllable *namaḥ*, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) as the object of address (*soddeśyaḥ*), and joined with the form (*rūpasaṃyutaḥ*). (2)
He himself, such as he is, the protector of the three worlds, [said]:
"O Lord of the Earth, grant me a calf; and when it is tamed, cause it to be given [to me] together with Svāhā. (3)
The other mantra of that [Varāha] consists of the seed-syllable *om* joined with its designation;
that same [designation] preceded by *namaḥ* and joined with the great word [*bhagavate*], and likewise joined with *svāhā*, is another mantra of Varāha. (4)

The unborn Hari, dark-complexioned, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his beautiful lower garment, accompanied by the Earth and all the objects mentioned as his own possessions,
and endowed with all his own forms— this Varāha should be meditated upon for the attainment of every desired goal.

For the Vaiṣṇavas, the sage is Brahmā; according to the distinction of the syllables of the mantras, the meter and the deity are to be known as one—the supreme Hari, who takes on those respective forms.
The wise know the six limbs [of the mantra] by means of the Praṇava, one's own name, Bhūdhara, Parātman, Sarvajña, and Sarvaśakti.
Alternatively, they know all the limbs of Viṣṇu as being filled by knowledge, sovereignty, splendor, bliss, majesty, and power, which reside within the center of the Self.
The eight-syllabled mantra beginning with "tiṣṭha," joined with "svāhā" and one's own name, brings prosperity and is a means for the constant remembrance of Him who is mounted upon Garuḍa. (9)
"Befrighten twice, terrify, and likewise crush;
then destroy and protect"—thus the five limbs are proclaimed.
"I myself bow down to the one who is full, heroic, vast Viṣṇu, the radiant one whose face is everywhere,
the lion among men, the terrifying yet auspicious one, and the slayer of Death"—
this is the thirty-two-syllable mantra of Hari. (11)
Above the word *dvirjaya*, one's own name [is placed], followed by *sodveṣam* and likewise *sarvavit*;
then *mahātejo balam vīryam* joined with *svāhā*. This twenty-four-syllable mantra bestows all desired objects. || 12 ||
"We know, we meditate" refers to what was previously [stated] and to the Greatly Powerful One himself;
"may He impel that for us"—this is proclaimed as Ananta in the middle. || 13 ||
The *aiṅga* [meter] is proclaimed to consist of both separate and combined feet;
among those, the first two have six syllables each as previously stated by the Omniscient One,
while the third consists of feet repeated twice, accompanied by the *aṅgas*.

One should meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, who has large, round, sun-like eyes; whose two hands are intent on drinking blood, while with the other two he holds a mace and a conch; who is united with his beloved; whose splendor exceeds ten million suns; and who possesses the foremost power. ||15||

For in all mantras, there is one who possesses arms numbering from two up to infinity; beginning with that which has consciousness as its innermost state, he possesses a form whose interior contains all limbs.
In this practice, the object of meditation should be formless, according to the instructions of one's own guru;
it should be visualized with appropriate weapons and ornaments, as is fitting and according to one's capacity.
The conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and shield; together with the bow Śārṅga, the arrow, the club, the ploughshare, the noose, and likewise the goad. (18)

The trident, the slingshot, the sword, fire, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the gesture of reasoning, the rosary, the book, and the act of rending— all these and every other [weapon] are to be meditated upon as being in the arms of Viṣṇu. (19)
"Viyaṭsa" consists of an even number of syllables and is known to be reversed;
it is devoid of the *sarga* (visarga), while "veta" is likewise [reversed] and lacks the nasal dot (*bindu*) at the end. (20)
These three great mantras are like wish-fulfilling trees for the four goals of human life; they are dear to Viṣṇu and bestow specialized knowledge.
By repeating those very [limbs] twice, their limbs are proclaimed;
the recitation in the form of breath is constant for both the wise and the ignorant. (22)
This great morning yoga, consisting of twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths] throughout day and night, should be constantly offered to Hari. (23)
It burns away all defects without exception, bestows the knowledge of reality, and grants the eightfold sovereign powers; it should be worshipped at the beginning of the Kṛta age.
The Tāra-yoga is likewise present from the very beginning, starting with Brahmā. (24)
One should meditate upon the Lord of Ramā, who possesses the splendor of a hundred thousand moons, whose hands are like the sun and moon, who is seated together with his beloved upon the lunar disc,
and whose two arms— bearing the conch and the lotus— are being sprinkled with nectar from the rising great orb of the moon.
The eternal Viṣṇu should be meditated upon as having a red color at the end,
or else he should be meditated upon as having the color of lightning, accompanied by Śakti and joined with the five mantras.
The great eight-syllable mantra, endowed with those very limbs and joined with the final meditation, bestows all human goals without exception. (27)
The root mantra consists of eighteen syllables: "pritaṣedha," together with its specific designation, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the enjoyers, joined with "svāhā. (28)
The Mantra-Cintāmaṇi itself provides its own limbs through those very words;
it bestows desired food, edibles, and so forth, and is the granter of liberation. (29)

One should meditate upon Him who is exceedingly white, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, who holds in His two arms a golden vessel containing curd-food and nectar, who is accompanied by all the gods, who is seated within the orb of the cool-rayed moon, and who is joined with Ramā. ||30||

The mantra "Amṛta" (Amṛte Amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtavarṣe amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarṣaṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā), consisting of eight syllables with the Tara (Om) prefixed, is endowed with its own specific injunctions; it is for the wise-hearted Manu (the practitioner), and its limbs (aṅgas) are formed by the words both individually and collectively.

Meditate upon Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the others; who possesses a face like that of the lord of gods with the radiance of the rising sun; who bears a mace and the embodiment of knowledge; who is unborn; who is united with his beloved; and who, by his own splendor, illuminates all space on every side.
Trivikrama, along with his manifestation, and Viśvarūpa beyond that; and Maheviṣṇu in the bestowal of wisdom—he who stands in the midst of our impulsion [is the goal]. 33.

The six-syllable mantra, consisting of the word *sanati* preceded by the initial syllables [of the deity's name] and joined with its own designation, is considered to be the ritual application of the limbs (*aṅga*) through its constituent letters. (34)
One should meditate upon that sole hero, who is charcoal-colored and surrounded on all sides by the radiance emanating from his body,
who bears an axe and a bow, and who— being praised by Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the other gods— is bestowing his own state of being.

One should remember the unconquered Lord, who is dark-complexioned and endowed with the splendor of the rays of twelve suns and the moon, who holds the bow and the arrow, who is united with his beloved,
who reveals his own immeasurable essential nature through the mouths of Hanumān and others, and who is praised with vast hymns.
One's own lineage (gotra), preceded by its location and the initial syllable, ending with a salutation and preceded by the *tāra* [Om], is considered the eight-syllabled mantra. (37)

And these, which are the seeds—the very essence of the seeds—of all phenomena (dharmas) without exception, are the victorious mantras that bestow knowledge and liberation; they are like celestial wish-fulfilling trees for those who desire gold, sons, kingdoms, and other such things. (38)
Kṛṣṇa, the protector of cows, the beloved, along with His location and the community of cowherd women;
the Beloved himself, accompanied by such [attendants]—this mantra of eighteen syllables bestows the limbs [of the ritual] through its words, granting love, desire, and liberation. (39)

One should meditate upon the Lord of Indirā, who resembles a sapphire, who is the sole object of worship for the world, the very essence of beauty, the unconquered one, and the bestower of all desired boons; he holds in his arms the lotus, the conch, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and is accompanied by the daughter of Bhīṣmaka and the goddess Tyasā.
This six-syllabled mantra, when preceded by the word *sakāmaḥ* (with desire), is itself the ultimate goal; it is proclaimed as the wish-fulfilling gem for all desired objects. || 41 ||
In the Kali age, the potency of mantras whose purpose is visible is obscured;
yet even there, mantras of blazing power are indeed proclaimed,
and among those, the mantras of the foremost of the Vasiṣṭhas and Vṛṣṇis bestow their power.
The eight-syllabled mantra, which is mounted upon the words of the Veda, preceded by the letter 'Pū', and ending with 'Na', is dear to the Lord of the Cow of Knowledge.
He bestows the qualities of eloquence, all-encompassing wisdom, and poetic skill;
he grants perpetual victory in debate, just as the Man-lion [grants victory] in battle. (44)
I bow with reverence to Vijñānarociḥ, who has filled the inner and outer cosmic eggs with a greenish-blue luster,
who is free from the fear of logic, and who bestows the wisdom of Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods.
We know and we meditate upon him who is filled with the city of knowledge and bliss;
may Vyāsa, the sovereign lord of the lords of mantras, impel us toward that. 46.
The primordial seed-syllable is the seed of stable knowledge regarding defects, bestowing liberation;
it causes the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all diseases. || 47 ||
One should meditate upon Him whose splendor of supreme bliss surpasses hundreds of millions of moons, who is being sprinkled by the lords of the gods with vast jars of nectar, and who,
together with the fifty letters presided over by Brahmā, Īśa, and the other deities, bestows all branches of knowledge.

But with its own twelve syllables, preceded by the long vowel [Ā] and joined with "Namaḥ," it is eight-syllabled; it bestows all vidyās, overcomes adversaries, is the means for liberation, and always grants fame, intelligence, and stability. (49)
I pay homage to the horse-headed one, who rests within the orb of the moon, white as the moon, illuminating the interior of the cosmic egg and its exterior on all sides with his infinite rays;
whose lotus-like arms are joined with the Śaṅkha, Akṣa, book, and the Subodha [scripture]. 50.
He was incessantly disgorging from his mouth the entirety of all branches of knowledge;
he was being served with extreme devotion by the foremost among the gods, such as Brahmā and Śiva; and he was constantly being sprinkled with the nectar of Lakṣmī.

The eight-syllable and nine-syllable mantras are traditionally remembered as consisting of the word *namaḥ* joined with the name preceded by its initial letter, followed by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*). || 52 ||
One should meditate upon Datta, who has a body equal to the rising sun, who has pervaded all the worlds with the vast rays of a thousand suns,
whose hands are marked with the symbols of knowledge and fearlessness, who is Kapila, who is accompanied by Aja and others, and who is awakening [the disciple].
These two [hymns] always bestow invincibility and the knowledge of liberation upon devotees;
they are the well-spoken hymn seen by Dīrghatamas and that of the Lord beginning with "viṣṇornu kam. (54)
The Gārtsamada hymn, which bestows all goals, and another, "yo jāta," as well as the Vāsiṣṭha hymn, "paro mātrayā," grant knowledge and liberation.
Even one who merely approaches this *Bhauvanīya*, which bestows all desires and liberation,
should understand that in this very same way, all the Vedas are devoted solely to Viṣṇu.
All that has been well-spoken by me is self-evident, bestowing desires and pleasing Hari;
it is the essence of the waters of speech, the limbs of Śrī, and Śrī, Lakṣmī, Mendirā, and Ramā.

One should meditate upon the Mother, whose garments are yellow silk, whose eyes are like lotuses, who holds two lotuses in her hands—one granting fearlessness and the other raised as a boon; she resembles the rising sun, is seated upon the supreme lap [of Śiva], and her pair of feet is worshipped by Brahmā and Īśvara. 58.
The seed-syllable of *lajjā* (hrīṃ) is its seed, and it is the designator of that very [goddess].
When placed upon red garments, the two syllables of *lajjā* are distinguished by the noose and the goad. (59)
The limb [of the mantra] situated in the non-midday, non-yugma, and non-sva positions has been thus illustrated; likewise, the sattā-bīja and the durbīja have been proclaimed.
The complexion is dark; the distinction here is that there is betel, a blue lotus, a conch, a discus, and a threatening gesture, while elsewhere there is a trident. 61.

The other mantra is remembered as that same one ending with "namas" and joined with its own [seed-syllable]. Durgā is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter, it is declared by Kaśyapa, and its color is remembered as being like fire. || 62 ||
The three-eyed nature of Durgā is generally described everywhere;
likewise, the body is said to consist of all the feet and the six armor-protecting parts (ṣaḍvarman).
For the learned know these to be indeed the forms of Ramā herself;
moreover, the son of Jamadagni is remembered as the presiding deity of this Manvantara.
The Hiraṇyagarbha-sūkta is proclaimed as having been seen by Bhṛgu;
it is declared that Brahmā, Dhātṛ, Viriñca, Aja, and Padma constitute its limbs.

One should meditate upon the unborn and undecaying one seated in the navel-lotus of Acyuta, supreme and resembling a mass of blazing suns; possessing hands of various forms and faces of unsurpassed beauty, he emits from all those mouths the sciences of the ultimate truth.
The five-syllable mantra of that [deity] is the pride of self-enunciation;
another such [mantra] is proclaimed to be eight-armed.
The *Bala* hymn and others are seen as the *sūkta* of the fire of life (*prāṇāgni*);
its limbs are also stated by the wise to consist of the five [elements] beginning with breath (*prāṇa*). (68)

One should meditate upon Him who resembles the radiance of the rising sun, seated comfortably on the lap of Acyuta, whose speech is constantly engaged in His praise, who holds a mace and the gesture of fearlessness in His hands, who has joined His palms in reverence, whose form is manifested at will, and whose power of action is exalted. (69)
The five mantras beginning with *prāṇa* are the designators of that deity;
by these, Hari himself—Nārāyaṇa and the others—is directly expressed. (70)
